thread.title: BlackBerry (BB) 4th Quarter Earnings: What to Expect

title: BlackBerry (BB) 4th Quarter Earnings: What to Expect
text:
BlackBerry (BB) 4th Quarter Earnings: What to Expect March 27, 2018, 07:57:17 AM EDT By Richard Saintvilus Shutterstock photo 
BlackBerry ( BB ) is set to report fourth quarter fiscal 2018 earnings results before the opening bell Wednesday. And Wall Street is eager to see if the extent to which the Canadian tech giant can monetize its recent deals. 
Shares have risen 15% year to date and 41% in six months, driven by a combination of factors, particularly is the company’s recent partnerships, affirming its strengths in the realm of automotive software. BlackBerry last Thursday reached a licensing agreement with Tata Motor's Jaguar Land Rover where the latter will use BlackBerry’s QNX infotainment and security software in their vehicles. But how much revenue and profits will this partnership - and others like it - generate? Analysts will seek to find out Wednesday. 
For the quarter that ended February, analysts expect BlackBerry to report breakeven adjusted earnings per share on revenue of $216.81 million. This compares to the year-ago quarter when earnings were 4 cents per share on $297 million in revenue. For the full year, earnings are projected to be 10 cents per share, up from 6 cents a year ago, while revenue of $938 million would decline 32% year over year. 
Thanks to better-than-expected fiscal third quarter earnings results and strong forward guidance, BlackBerry shares have rallied out of their flat range. But the company, which has conceded the mobile hardware market to Apple ( AAPL ) and Samsung ( SSNLF ), must figure out a way to get revenue growing again. Over the past three quarters, revenue have declined by an average of 30%. And this quarter’s expected 27% decline won’t help reverse the trend. 
“We really do have a lot of people that want to do business with us,” CEO John Chen said in an interview. Investors, however, would be more confident if BlackBerry’s top line reflected Chen’s confidence. The company’s revenues ha been in a steady decline since its 2011 fiscal year. While third quarter revenue of $235 million easily topped the Street estimate of $215 million, it still reflected a 22% decline. 
On the bright side, BlackBerry has become a cash-generating machine. At the end of the third quarter, BlackBerry’s cash equivalents, and investments stood at about $2.5 billion, leading to a net cash balance of about $1.9 billion when excluding $605 million for its debt. And BlackBerry now has an arsenal of security products that has brought in contracts from the likes of NATO and the U.S. Justice and Defense Department. 
Elsewhere, the company recently announced an agreement with Microsoft ( MSFT ) to increase security on mobile phones, allowing mobile users to open Microsoft mobile apps from BlackBerry Dynamics, a secure container for mobile apps. The agreement also allows for enterprise users to access Microsoft Office 365 files in Excel, PowerPoint and Word on both iOs and Android devices. 
It remains to be seen how these agreements boost BlackBerry’s top- and bottom lines over the next couple of years. One thing is certain though, the company has successfully transitioned away from hardware to software. And how it executes on these deals will determine how much premium BB stock deserves from here.
